title: How does an octopus change colour in a blink?
hook: It matches the colour of the seabed, yet it most likely can’t see colour.
summary: Octopus skin is packed with pigment sacs called chromatophores, stretched open by nerve-controlled muscles; the puzzle is that octopuses appear to be colour-blind.
cardText: Thousands of pigment sacs in its skin, stretched open by nerve-controlled muscles, let an octopus change colour almost instantly. The mystery: most studies suggest it can’t see colour at all.

cardBlocks.text: Picture a screen where every pixel is a tiny balloon of ink. Octopus skin works a bit like that, with about 230 chromatophores per square millimetre. Each one is an elastic sac of pigment ringed by 15 to 25 muscle fibres, wired to nerves that run straight from the brain. When the muscles contract, the sac flattens from about 10 to about 300 micrometres (thousandths of a millimetre) across and colours that patch of skin.

Because nerves and muscles do the work, the change is almost instantaneous, and no other animals match octopuses, squid and cuttlefish for speed of colour change. Yet an octopus eye has only one visual pigment, and most studies conclude that it cannot tell colours apart. How it matches the colour of its background is still an open question.
Octopuses change colour with pigment sacs pulled open by muscles and nerves, apparently without being able to see colour.

deepDiveBlocks.text: A 2016 proposal looks at the shape of the pupil. Each colour comes into focus at a slightly different distance behind the lens, an effect called chromatic aberration. With an off-centre pupil, like those of most shallow-water cephalopods, an animal could work out colour from focus, even with a single type of photoreceptor. Other researchers have questioned the idea.

Scientists found that pieces of octopus skin, cut away from the body, open their chromatophores when light hits them, fastest under blue light. The skin makes the same light-sensitive protein (opsin) used in the eyes, and the authors suggest this may play a part in camouflage. Supporters of the pupil idea point out that, with the same opsin as the eye, the skin responds to light almost exactly like the retina, so it would not solve the colour puzzle.

Changing colour costs energy. A study measured the oxygen used by octopus skin and estimated that the fully activated chromatophore system burns nearly as much as the whole animal at rest. The authors suggest this cost may have favoured night-time habits and the use of dens.
